opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think there's a real continuity there, but it's not a one-to-one replacement. The way I think about it, human data labeling was about capturing judgments. You'd have someone look at two completions and say which one is better, or write out an ideal answer, and that becomes a static artifact you train on. That was hugely important for getting models to where they are, especially for things like instruction following and tone.

But once you move into RL, especially for agentic tasks, what you actually need isn't just a pile of labeled examples. You need a world for the model to act in. You need the tools, the task distribution, the verification logic, the reward signal. An environment is a much richer object than a dataset. It's closer to software than it is to annotation.

So in one sense, yes, it's the successor, because it's where a lot of the marginal value in post-training is going, and a lot of the companies that did data work are naturally moving in that direction. But the skill set shifts. It's less about managing a large workforce of labelers and more about engineering: understanding a domain well enough to build a realistic task, figuring out how to grade it robustly so the model can't just reward-hack its way through, and making sure the difficulty is calibrated so there's actually signal to learn from.

And humans don't go away. You still need people with real domain expertise designing the tasks and checking whether the rewards actually track what you care about. But their leverage is much higher. One well-designed environment can generate an enormous amount of training signal, whereas a labeled example is used once. So I see it less as replacing human data and more as humans moving up a level of abstraction, from producing the answers to building the systems that judge the answers.

r001.rationale: The response says humans remain involved in designing tasks and checking rewards, but it does not explain that RL environments sustain demand for human data because they target capabilities models have not yet mastered.

r002.rationale: It mentions using domain expertise to design tasks and check rewards, but does not identify finding what humans can uniquely contribute to improving model skills as the key design problem.

r003.rationale: The response mentions verification logic, reward signals, and grading, but does not describe deriving reward scores from yes/no judgments of whether an answer meets task-success criteria.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think that's roughly right, but with a caveat. The thing Scale did really well was turn human judgment into a product: you need a million labeled examples, here's a pipeline, here's quality control, here's a price. And for a while that was the bottleneck. Pretraining data was free, basically, and the scarce thing was good supervised fine-tuning and preference data.

What's changed is that the models are now good enough that a lot of the value isn't in showing them the answer, it's in giving them a place to try things and get feedback. So the scarce input shifts from "a human wrote the ideal response" to "here's a task, here's a way to check whether you did it, go." That's an environment. And the people who are good at building those look a lot more like software engineers than annotators. You're writing a harness, you're writing a verifier, you're thinking about how to make the reward signal hard to game.

But I'd push back on the idea that it fully replaces the human labeling business. A few reasons. One, environments still need humans to define what good looks like, especially for anything subjective or open-ended. The rubric has to come from somewhere. Two, the long tail of real-world tasks is enormous, and most of them don't have a clean programmatic check. Coding and math are the easy cases. Three, a lot of what Scale sells now is evaluation, red-teaming, and expert data, and that doesn't go away. If anything, you need more of it, because once you're doing RL you need to know whether the thing you optimized is actually what you wanted.

So I'd say it's a successor in the sense that it's where the marginal dollar is going. The labor is different, it's more leveraged, and it compounds in a way labeling never did, because a good environment can produce unlimited training signal. But I'd frame it less as "environments replace labels" and more as "the stack moves up a level." You used to pay people to produce data. Now you pay people to produce the machinery that produces data, and you still need humans in the loop at the top to say what the machinery should be optimizing for.

The open question to me is whether that becomes a real third-party market the way labeling did, or whether the labs just build it all in-house. My guess is it ends up somewhere in between. The frontier labs will own the environments that matter most to them, and there'll be a big open and commercial ecosystem for everything else, because there's just too much surface area for any one org to cover.

r001.rationale: The response says humans define what good looks like and that many tasks lack clean programmatic checks, but it does not connect ongoing human-data demand to targeting capabilities models have not yet mastered.

r002.rationale: The response says humans define rubrics and guide what machinery should optimize, but it does not identify finding the information humans uniquely contribute to improving model skills as the key design problem.

r003.rationale: The response mentions verifiers and reward signals, but does not describe turning yes/no judgments about task success into a reward score.

astra-6.text:
Yeah, I think in some sense it is. With human data labeling, you’re often asking someone to provide the right answer or demonstrate what good behavior looks like. With an RL environment, you’re building a setting where the model can try things and get feedback on whether they worked. So the human effort moves toward defining the task, setting up the tools, and figuring out how to evaluate success.

But I wouldn’t say labeling just goes away. There are plenty of tasks where you still need human judgment to tell whether an outcome is good. The interesting shift is from producing individual examples to building something that can support lots of attempts and learning. And the hard part is making sure that what the environment rewards actually matches what you want the model to do.

sol-6.1.text:
Yeah, I think there’s a pretty natural progression there. With supervised fine-tuning, you’re asking a person to demonstrate what good behavior looks like. With reinforcement learning, you’re building a setup where the model can try things and get feedback on whether they worked. So the human work shifts from writing the answer to defining the task, setting up the environment, and figuring out what success means.

Coding is a good example: you need a repository, a task, and tests that actually distinguish a correct solution from something that just looks plausible. The model can then make many attempts without a human grading every one. But constructing that environment still takes judgment. Are the tests sufficient? Can the model exploit the grading? Does solving the task teach something useful?

So I’d call it an evolution of the data business. You’re producing opportunities for the model to learn through interaction, and the quality of those opportunities matters a lot.
